extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, students, and news professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the criteria, values, and institutional constraints journalists use when selecting and producing national news — covering professional values, working conditions, commercial pressures, and audience research. Useful for analyzing newsworthiness and newsroom decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring professional values
rubrics_metrics.description: Values that are part of the journalists' workplace and built into news judgment (not merely personal beliefs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'enduring values' pull journalists toward particular choices even when work requirements push otherwise. Examples/phrases from text: suspicion of oratory and grand plans, bias toward pragmatism and common sense, appreciation of 'competent and honest men,' hardness toward 'scoundrels and buffoons,' commitment to rational programs, and opposition to violence. John Chancellor's quote is used as an exemplar of these traits. The chapter argues these values cannot be omitted from explanations of story selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source productivity and efficiency as a selection criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists emphasize sources who are productive and efficient (e.g., the president) because such sources reliably provide usable copy. "They emphasize the president ... because he is a productive and efficient source of news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instrumental standard pushes journalists to privilege certain officials and regular sources; it can bias coverage toward accessible elites and official perspectives rather than marginalized participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic news / novelty as newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Social disorder and other events are reported because they are dramatic and therefore 'newsworthy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations expect dramatic material; reporters 'report social disorder because they are expected to deliver dramatic news.' This dynamic can lead stories to side with restorers of order rather than participants, shaping frame and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation / open-mindedness / objectivity norm
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional norm that journalists should be 'open-minded' and moderate, often expressed as occupying the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderation is partly defensive (safer to be near the center when criticized from both sides). Journalists describe themselves as 'classic liberal' or middle-of-the-road; moderation influences tone and selection. Example: If receiving critical mail from both 'Nazis' and 'Communists', journalists felt no need to worry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberties as an instrumental journalistic value
rubrics_metrics.description: High value placed on civil liberties because journalistic autonomy and freedom of the press depend on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as an instrumental necessity: protecting civil liberties preserves reporters' ability to operate independently. It informs editorial positions on issues affecting press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Communism/ideological workplace constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A workplace value/attitude (anti-communism) that partly stems from professional definitions of autonomy and who counts as a professional journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because American professionals define autonomy differently than Communist journalists, anti-Communist views may be embedded in practice and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antipathy to bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists tend to dislike bureaucracy, a disposition rooted partly in their organizational position as (often unwilling) members of bureaucratic news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disposition affects how bureaucratic actors and structures are covered, often producing skeptical or critical reporting about bureaucracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern with responsible leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: A value that favors reporting which emphasizes responsible leadership, influenced by the central role of top editors, producers, and executives in journalists' work lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because newsroom hierarchies shape morale and production, stories often privilege themes of competent leadership and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewarding individualism and productive individualists
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations reward the productive individualist; individualistic career ideals (e.g., freelance work) influence norms and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disposition favors stories and personnel that showcase individual initiative and productivity. It also shapes staffing preferences and cultural norms within newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality judgments shaped by a limited set of sources and social similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic judgments about what is 'real' derive partly from a relatively small, socially similar aggregate of sources used regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even adversarial reporting often relies on sources similar in social, economic, and cultural backgrounds to journalists. Consequence: limited contact with different social groups (e.g., working class) produces skewed conceptions (examples: 'hard hats', Archie Bunker) and affects story framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of normality from upper-middle-class experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' expectations of normal everyday behavior often reflect upper-middle-class standards and experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: emphasis on 'urban revitalization' because journalists notice gentrifiers more than the majority of urban homeowners. These norms are routinely translated into story ideas and universalized in magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal experience and background influence news judgments (but do not wholly determine them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal childhood and adult experiences shape some reality judgments and values journalists use in determining newsworthiness, although enduring professional values also operate independent of personal beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes that while personal experience matters, enduring newsroom values are built into judgment processes; journalists can accept these values even if they don't hold them personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class and education of journalists as a determinant of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The social class and educational backgrounds (largely upper-middle-class, college-educated) of national journalists influence their perspectives and the kinds of stories they produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data and examples (salaries, school backgrounds) illustrate that most national journalists are upwardly mobile, often from middle-class origins; this shared background helps explain acceptance of enduring values and certain audience assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from business departments
rubrics_metrics.description: An institutional norm: editorial and business departments operate largely independently; business can propose but not directly control editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business departments want influence to boost audience and advertisers but typically cannot interfere. Corporate management may persuade journalists to heed economic well-being, but historical examples (e.g., Saturday Evening Post) show editors remaining free to make editorial choices despite commercial pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between commercial considerations and audience considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial considerations aim to reduce costs or increase revenue; audience considerations aim to maintain or hold the present audience and may be applied for reasons beyond pure commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists pay little direct attention to audience size and even less to costs/profits. The text distinguishes the two pressures and describes how journalists respond differently to each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget/cost constraints affect production but not necessarily story selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Top producers must consider costs and live within budgets, leading to cost-cutting (reducing ancillary services, moving deadlines) but important stories still get covered because of competition and prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cutbacks during stagflation; back-of-book deadlines advanced (affecting timeliness of some pieces), reductions in editorial staff at Time, and retention of costly coverage for major breaking stories despite budget pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies to increase revenue: enlarge or upgrade audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Two commercial tactics: enlarging audience size (networks) and upgrading readership quality/income (magazines) to increase advertising revenue or ad rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines often seek 'upscale' readers (younger, more affluent) and sometimes deliberately discourage 'downscale' readers (e.g., omitting detailed explanations). Networks try format changes, anchor hires, or affiliate persuasion — often with limited success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of sensationalism and 'show business' formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and many editors object to sensationalist content, 'happy news,' and overt show-business techniques, seeing them as lowering journalistic standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text details journalistic resistance to sensationalism (crime/sex exploitation), informal on-air banter, and celebrity-driven hires; journalists publicly criticize such moves and prefer to distance editorial content from entertainment formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover selection balancing importance and commercial appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsmagazine cover decisions weigh journalistic importance against potential newsstand sales; importance considerations generally take precedence though covers may be chosen for sales occasionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers are expected to maximize newsstand sales, but editors prioritize importance (e.g., a breaking foreign story will make the cover even if sales are poor). Sex covers sell well but are used sparingly (once every three or four years) to avoid being seen as 'going commercial.' Newsstand sales are treated as a feedback signal but are imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience research reliance and methodological limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks and magazines rely on commercial research organizations (e.g., Simmons, Nielsen); methods (diaries, interviews) measure reported viewing/reading but cannot fully capture attention or partial/segmentary consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations include reliance on self-reports ('looked at' a program), pass-along readers in magazines, and the inability to know how much of content people actually attended to. Journalists are wary of audience research and often find it unhelpful for guiding editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience demographic targeting influences content and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in audience demographics between media (magazines vs TV) shape editorial style and content choices: magazines skew toward a younger, more educated/upscale readership while TV news serves an older audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simmons data illustrate median age and education/income differences; magazines may omit explanatory detail for upscale readers, and television content may be tailored toward older viewers' preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer norms discourage obvious commercialism ('going commercial')
rubrics_metrics.description: Norms among journalists and editors disfavor overtly commercial editorial choices; being seen as 'going commercial' draws peer criticism and morale effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may suspect superiors of 'going commercial' but are reluctant to admit commercial motives; peer criticism acts as an informal check on commercial coverages or formats.
